# How to Set, Name and Check Kitchen Timers by Voice on Your Alexa Echo

> **In short:** You can set several named cooking timers on an Echo speaker by voice, check the time left on each one, and cancel them without touching a phone. Your Echo must be set up and online, and the exact wording can vary by device.

By the end of this guide, you'll be able to run three or four cooking timers at once, each with its own name, while your hands stay busy with dough, a whisk or a hot pan. It's written for people who already use Alexa for simple things like weather and music, and who want the kitchen to run a little more smoothly.

## Before you start
- An Amazon account linked to an Echo speaker in the Alexa app, with the Echo connected to Wi-Fi. You don't need to set anything else up.
- Alexa+ (Amazon's newer, more conversational version of Alexa) may need an Amazon Prime membership or a separate paid plan, depending on your country and account. Check the Alexa app or Amazon's official Alexa page for what your account includes. The timer steps below work with the standard Alexa voice commands.
- Plan on about 15 minutes to practice. Keep a pot of water or a bowl nearby so you can test without cooking anything.

## Step 1 — Set your first timer with a name
Stand where your voice carries well, then say the wake word (by default, "Alexa") followed by the timer request. Speak naturally, in one short sentence, and include a name such as "pasta" or "rice." Your Echo's light ring usually lights up when it hears you, and it answers out loud with a confirmation like a timer set for a certain number of minutes. If your Echo has a screen, a small timer card often appears too. If it only asks which timer you mean, repeat the request with the name at the end.

Naming the timer matters later, because it's how you'll find it again when several are running. Many people find that naming a timer after the dish works better than generic names like "timer one."

💬 Example: "Alexa, set a [dish name] timer for [number] minutes."

You'll know it worked when Alexa confirms the timer by its name and length, and the timer starts counting down.

## Step 2 — Add a second timer while the first one runs
Keep the first timer running, then give Alexa another named request in the same way. The point is to avoid guessing which pot is which. Alexa keeps each timer separate, so the second request doesn't cancel or replace the first one. Give the second timer a clearly different name, like "rice" or "sauce," so you won't confuse them when they finish.

If Alexa asks whether you want to replace the existing timer, it's usually because the names are too similar or the request was unclear. Say "No, keep it" or simply repeat the new request with a distinct name. If your Echo doesn't allow a second timer at the same time, you'll hear a message saying so. In that case, you'll need to cancel one first, which is covered in Step 4.

💬 Example: "Alexa, set a [second dish name] timer for [number] minutes."

You'll know it worked when Alexa confirms the second timer and both are counting down. Your Echo will alert you separately for each one when its time is up.

## Step 3 — Check how much time is left on each timer
Whenever you're unsure, ask. You can check one timer by name or ask Alexa to list what's running. Speak in a normal voice from wherever you are in the kitchen. Alexa answers with the time remaining, such as minutes and seconds left on that one timer. If your Echo has a screen, the timers may also appear on it, though you don't need the screen to hear the answer.

This is a helpful habit when you step away from the stove to chop vegetables or check the oven. You don't have to remember the start time in your head, because Alexa keeps track of it for you. If Alexa answers with a timer you didn't expect, check the name. It may be the one you set earlier with a similar name.

💬 Example: "Alexa, how much time is left on my [dish name] timer?"

You'll know it worked when Alexa reads back a specific amount of time for the named timer, and that number gets smaller each time you ask again later.

## Step 4 — Cancel or replace a timer by name
Sometimes plans change. The water boils faster than expected, or you decide to bake instead of simmer. You can stop a timer by name, and then set a fresh one with the new time. Say the cancel request clearly, including the name, so Alexa stops only the timer you mean. Alexa will usually confirm that it has canceled the timer.

Some Echo devices and Alexa+ may also let you adjust a running timer, such as adding a minute, but that wording varies. If you aren't sure, the safest approach is to cancel the timer and set a new one with the right length. Doing so takes only a few seconds and keeps the names and times accurate.

💬 Example: "Alexa, cancel my [dish name] timer."

You'll know it worked when Alexa confirms the cancellation, and when you ask about that timer again, it says there's no timer with that name.

## Step 5 — Turn a recipe into a timer list
This is where Alexa+ is most useful for a more advanced kitchen workflow. Instead of working out every time in your head, you describe the dish and ask Alexa+ to list the steps that need a timer, in the order you'll reach them. You then set each timer yourself using Steps 1 and 2. Alexa+ can answer in a conversational way, so you can follow up with questions like "Which of those can I start at the same time?"

Treat the list as a rough draft. Compare every number with your own recipe or the package instructions before you rely on it. Alexa+ cannot see your pot, your oven, or the food itself, so it can't tell you when something is actually done. Use your recipe and your own checks, such as a food thermometer for meat, to decide when food is ready.

💬 Example: "I'm making [dish name] for [number] people. List the steps that need a timer, with the minutes for each, in the order I'll reach them."

You'll know it worked when Alexa+ gives you a short, numbered list of steps with times, and you can read each item back and set the matching timer by name.

## Common mistakes
- **Using names that sound alike.** "Pasta" and "pasta water" can be heard as the same name, so Alexa may pick the wrong timer. Fix it by choosing names that are clearly different, such as "pasta" and "sauce."
- **Trusting Alexa+'s times without checking.** A suggested cooking time can be off for your ingredients, your pan or your altitude. Fix it by comparing every number with your recipe and checking doneness yourself.
- **Expecting Alexa to watch the food.** Alexa only counts time. It can't see smoke, bubbling or browning, and it can't tell you when something is safe to eat. Fix it by keeping an eye on the food and using a reliable doneness check, like a thermometer where it applies.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** Set a named timer for each part of dinner, then ask "how much time is left" while you prep. You'll spend less time reading the clock and more time cooking.
- **For your business or work:** If you cook for a family event, a small catering job, or a shared kitchen, a short list of named timers can keep several dishes on schedule without writing everything on a whiteboard.
- **If you want to go further:** Look in the Alexa app for a section called Routines, which may let you link several voice actions together. Routines and their options vary by device and account, so check what your app offers before you plan around them.

## Try it now
Within the next two minutes, say "Alexa, set a [dish name] timer for [number] minutes," then say "Alexa, set a [second dish name] timer for [number] minutes." Finish by asking "Alexa, how much time is left on my [dish name] timer?" If all three answers come back the way the steps describe, your kitchen timers are ready for a real meal.
